questions.stem: A California prescriber issued an otherwise valid methylphenidate prescription six days ago. The patient presents it today at a Massachusetts pharmacy. Which threshold issue is dispositive?

choices.text: California is outside the narcotic contiguous-state list.
Methylphenidate becomes Schedule VI when issued outside Massachusetts.
The prescription is eligible because nonnarcotic Schedule II prescriptions have no timing gate.
The Massachusetts five-day presentation window has passed.

questions.stem: During a pharmacy-system configuration audit, the pharmacist reviews rules that would automatically control dispensing or monitoring. Which configurations are legally correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Treat pregabalin as Schedule V and submit covered dispensing to MassPAT.
Treat gabapentin as federally noncontrolled but Massachusetts Schedule VI and MassPAT-reportable.
Treat methylphenidate as Schedule II and block prescription refills.
Apply CMEA retail-sale controls to pseudoephedrine without classifying it as Schedule V solely because of those controls.
Apply the federal Schedule III-IV five-refill/six-month rule to gabapentin solely because Massachusetts places it in Schedule VI.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives a Focalin prescription issued four days ago by a properly registered New Hampshire prescriber. The pharmacist verifies the prescription and prescriber. Which conclusion is most defensible?

choices.text: Reject it because all out-of-state Schedule II prescriptions are prohibited.
Apply the five-day contiguous-state narcotic rule because all Schedule II drugs are narcotics.
Dispense under the nonnarcotic Schedule II out-of-state pathway after verification.
Use the 30-day out-of-state Schedule III-through-VI window.
Dispense without verification because New Hampshire is contiguous.

questions.stem: An adult patient receives a lawful 14-day outpatient prescription for buprenorphine-naloxone specifically for treatment of opioid use disorder. A staff member says Massachusetts' seven-day initial-opiate statute automatically requires the prescription to be reduced to seven days. What is the best response to that specific claim?

choices.text: Agree, because every medication related to an opioid is subject to the seven-day statute regardless of indication.

Disagree. The seven-day statute expressly does not apply to medications designed for treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence; the prescription must instead satisfy the other laws governing its OUD pathway.
Agree unless the patient has previously filled an opioid prescription in Massachusetts.
Disagree because buprenorphine-naloxone becomes Massachusetts Schedule VI when used for OUD.
Reduce the quantity to seven days without prescriber involvement because pharmacists may unilaterally rewrite any opioid prescription to comply with supply limits.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts practitioner issues an adult patient's first outpatient oxycodone prescription for a 10-day supply after an acute fracture. The practitioner documents in the medical record that more than seven days are required for the acute condition and that a non-opiate alternative is not appropriate. What is the most accurate conclusion about the seven-day statute?

choices.text: The prescription must still be limited to seven days because no exception can apply to an adult's first outpatient opiate prescription.
The documented statutory exception can permit the quantity needed for the acute condition; the seven-day ceiling is not absolute on these facts.
The exception applies only if the patient is a minor.
The exception applies automatically to every Schedule II prescription without documentation.
A pharmacist may create the missing medical-record documentation after dispensing if the prescriber did not do so.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old patient has received opiates before and now presents a 10-day Norco prescription for outpatient dental pain. No statutory exception is documented. A staff member says the seven-day rule no longer applies because this is not the minor's first opiate prescription. What should the pharmacist recognize?

choices.text: The staff member is correct; the minor rule applies only to a first opiate prescription, just like the adult rule.
The staff member is incorrect; the minor provision generally limits an opiate prescription to seven days at any time unless a statutory exception is properly documented.
The 10-day quantity becomes permissible if a parent signs the prescription at pickup.
The Schedule II quantity rule automatically overrides the minor-specific seven-day provision.
Prior opioid exposure converts the patient to the adult first-prescription rule even though the patient is still a minor.

questions.stem: At a Massachusetts pharmacy, a fentanyl prescription from a Rhode Island practitioner was issued four days ago and the pharmacist obtains direct verification. What Massachusetts rule is central?

choices.text: Use the 30-day out-of-state Schedule III-through-VI window.
Fill any state's Schedule II narcotic prescription within five days.
Skip direct verification because Rhode Island is contiguous.
Treat electronic transmission as resetting the five-day issue period.
Apply the contiguous-state Schedule II narcotic pathway and its five-day and verification conditions.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives an Ativan prescription issued 20 days ago by a properly authorized Connecticut practitioner. The pharmacist verifies the prescription and prescriber. What is the key determination?

choices.text: Reject it after five days under the Schedule II narcotic rule.
The prescription falls within the 30-day out-of-state Schedule IV pathway after verification.
Use the federal six-month clock as the only deadline.
Accept it without verification because Connecticut licenses the practitioner.
Require a Massachusetts prescriber for every Schedule IV prescription.

questions.stem: A Klonopin prescription states six refills, and the pharmacy has already dispensed five refills within five months. What should the pharmacist recognize about the requested sixth refill?

choices.text: Honor the sixth refill because it appears on the original.
Count only refills dispensed in Massachusetts.
Federal law limits Schedule IV prescriptions to five refills within six months, despite the prescriber's notation.
Allow another refill because five months is less than six months.
Convert the sixth refill into a partial fill of the fifth.

questions.stem: During prospective legal review, an unfilled electronic Librium prescription has already been transferred once at the patient's request. The patient now seeks a second transfer. What is the result?

choices.text: Permit a second transfer because no dose has been dispensed.
Print and fax it so the next transaction is no longer electronic.
Return it to the original pharmacy and treat that return as a refill.
Allow another transfer when the patient consents in writing.
Do not transfer it a second time under the federal one-time electronic controlled-prescription rule.

questions.stem: A Halcion prescription is five months old and has already been refilled five times. Which fact prevents another refill?

choices.text: Dispense because the six-month period remains open.
The five-refill maximum is exhausted even though the six-month period has not ended.
Treat five completed refills as five new prescriptions.
Add a refill after confirming stable therapy with the patient.
Apply the no-refill rule used for Schedule II drugs.

questions.stem: A patient presents an otherwise authentic out-of-state Ambien prescription 31 days after issue. What is the Massachusetts consequence?

choices.text: Fill it because federal Schedule IV authority lasts six months.
Use the five-day contiguous-state narcotic rule.
Accept the prescription after telephone verification on day 31.
The Massachusetts 30-day out-of-state window has expired.
Change the issue date to the date the pharmacy received it.

questions.stem: A patient requests transfer of an unfilled electronic Sonata prescription to a second DEA-registered retail pharmacy. Both pharmacists can communicate directly. What else must be confirmed?

choices.text: Confirm no prior transfer, preserve the electronic record, and verify state permission.
Transfer it even if the original prescription was paper.
Permit repeated transfers until the first dispensing.
Let a technician transmit the record without pharmacist communication.
Ignore Massachusetts transfer restrictions because federal permission preempts every state condition.

questions.stem: An adult patient's first outpatient tramadol prescription for acute pain requests a 10-day supply and contains no facts supporting a statutory exception. A technician argues that the Massachusetts seven-day opiate rule cannot apply because tramadol is Schedule IV rather than Schedule II. Which conclusion is most accurate?

choices.text: The technician is correct because the seven-day statute applies only to Schedule II narcotic prescriptions.
The technician is correct because Massachusetts excludes every Schedule IV drug from opiate supply limits.
The prescription is exempt whenever the patient pays cash.
The pharmacy may ignore the supply issue if MassPAT was checked.
The technician is incorrect; Schedule IV status does not exempt tramadol from the separate seven-day opiate rule.

questions.stem: During an end-of-shift check, a pharmacy receives its first DEA registration and will begin stocking controlled substances tomorrow. What inventory event is required?

choices.text: Take the first inventory at the end of the first month.
Wait two years because only biennial inventories are required.
Inventory only Schedule II stock on the start date.
Take an initial inventory of controlled substances on the date controlled-substance activity begins.
Use the wholesaler's invoice as the pharmacy's initial inventory.

questions.stem: At a Massachusetts pharmacy, a pharmacy took its last complete controlled-substance inventory 25 months ago. What is the issue?

choices.text: No problem exists until 30 months have elapsed.
The annual pharmacy permit renewal resets the inventory clock.
Only Schedule II stock needs a biennial inventory.
A perpetual inventory removes the need for the biennial snapshot.
The federal biennial inventory interval has been exceeded.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy technician trainee is performing data-entry work while a pharmacist is directly supervising the trainee. At pickup, the patient asks whether the new medication can be taken with warfarin, and the profile shows an unresolved DUR alert. Which actions are appropriate for the trainee? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Collect and enter nonclinical demographic information while remaining under direct pharmacist supervision.
Counsel the patient on the interaction after reading the drug-information screen.
Perform authorized prescription-processing and staging tasks under direct pharmacist supervision, while leaving final verification to the pharmacist.
Continue other authorized clerical or technical trainee functions while under direct pharmacist supervision.
Refer the clinical question and unresolved DUR issue to the pharmacist rather than exercising pharmacist professional judgment.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is assigning staff to receive Schedule II stock. The pharmacist has approved written policies and procedures. Which statements correctly distinguish the current technician pathways? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A registered pharmacy technician may assist with transporting Schedule II stock under pharmacist supervision.
A registered pharmacy technician who is not certified may assist with Schedule II transport under pharmacist supervision but does not thereby gain the certified technician's broader handling role.
A certified pharmacy technician may assist with transporting and handling Schedule II stock under pharmacist supervision when the pharmacy's approved policies permit it.
A pharmacy technician trainee may independently assume Schedule II accountability because trainee registration is enough to replace pharmacist oversight.
The pharmacist remains responsible for Schedule II accountability, security, and professional judgment even when authorized support personnel assist.

questions.stem: A pharmacy schedules an intern for a shift without a pharmacist preceptor directing the work. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A senior technician may serve as the preceptor.
The intern must work under direct supervision of a registered pharmacist preceptor.
Five hundred internship hours permit independent prescription verification.
Intern status does not authorize independent pharmacist practice.
The pharmacist preceptor remains responsible for the supervision relationship.

questions.stem: A pharmacy student completes 12 hours of qualifying Massachusetts pharmacy-internship activity in one day. The student then remains at the site for a separate two-hour school seminar, and the preceptor proposes recording all 14 hours as Board internship credit. What should be recorded? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The preceptor should record no more than 12 qualifying internship hours for that day.
No more than 12 hours may be credited toward the pharmacy internship in one day.
The extra seminar may be documented separately as school activity, but it cannot increase that day's Board internship credit.
Combining internship work with separately documented educational activity does not raise the Board's maximum internship credit above 12 hours for that day.
All 14 hours may count as internship credit whenever the preceptor signs both the internship log and the seminar attendance record.

questions.stem: A pharmacist plans continuing education for the two-year Massachusetts renewal cycle. Which statements are generally correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Complete at least 20 contact hours in each calendar year.
Include at least two contact hours of pharmacy law each calendar year.
Use no more than 15 home-study hours in a calendar year absent an exception.
Carry unused hours freely into the next calendar year.
Do not carry unused annual hours into the next calendar year.

questions.stem: A pharmacist directly oversees both sterile and complex nonsterile compounding. Which continuing-education statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Meet the applicable annual sterile-compounding CE requirement.
Use general pharmacy-law CE in place of all compounding CE.
Also assess the annual complex-nonsterile compounding CE requirement.
Apply compounding CE only to technicians.
Treat the applicable requirements as cumulative when both activities are supervised.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is evaluating the current statutory qualifications to enter a collaborative practice agreement. Which statements reflect M.G.L. c.112, § 24B1/2(b)? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Hold a current Massachusetts pharmacist license, currently practice in the Commonwealth, and maintain at least $1,000,000 of professional liability insurance.
Have earned a PharmD degree or completed five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist, or the equivalent.
Devote a portion of practice to the defined drug-therapy area and complete at least five additional related CE contact hours in each agreement year.
Apply for the statute's limited MassHealth ordering/referring participation if implementing regulations governing that participation are promulgated.
A pharmacist with a current PharmD must also complete five years of licensed-practice experience because the degree alternative is no longer recognized by statute.

questions.stem: A retail collaborative program receives a physician referral for an adult patient who has not yet consented. Which limits apply before the pharmacist acts? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Obtain the required patient notice and consent.
Stay within the agreement, referral, authorized disease states, and retail scope.
Use the written agreement and supervising-physician framework.
Diagnose an unrelated disease independently.
Enroll any walk-in patient automatically.

questions.stem: A proposed retail collaborative agreement would let a pharmacist prescribe alprazolam and methylphenidate. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: $1,000,000 liability coverage waives the schedule restriction.
Only Schedule II prescribing is prohibited.
The agreement cannot authorize prescribing Schedule II through V drugs.
A supervising physician's signature does not remove that prohibition.
Schedule VI prescribing requires separate compliance with retail CDTM limits.

questions.stem: A retail collaborating pharmacist issues an authorized Schedule VI prescription for the patient's referred diagnosis. Which actions are required? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Add Schedule II refills under the same agreement.
Keep the prescription within the diagnosis and agreement scope.
Send a copy to the supervising physician within 24 hours.
Delay physician notice until the agreement is renewed.
Document the prescription in the patient's collaborative-practice record.

questions.stem: Before dispensing a new prescription, a Massachusetts pharmacist's prospective review identifies a clinically significant interaction. Which actions are consistent with the current prospective drug-review duty? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Let a technician independently resolve the interaction if the dispensing software supplies a recommended override code.
Skip prospective review because the prescriber sent the prescription electronically.
Ensure the pharmacist conducts prospective drug review before the new prescription is dispensed or delivered.
Automatically refuse every prescription that generates an alert without considering the specific problem or communicating when appropriate.
Take appropriate measures to resolve an identified therapy problem, which may include consultation with the prescriber or patient and documentation of the measures taken.

questions.stem: At pickup of a new prescription, the pharmacist or designee makes the required offer to counsel and the patient declines. Which Massachusetts documentation statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Reasonable efforts to obtain, record, and maintain patient information include recording a patient's failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel.
The refusal information may be recorded in the patient profile, prescription signature log, or another system of records.
If there is no record that the patient failed to accept the offer, the statute creates a presumption that counseling was provided.
A notarized waiver is not required; the refusal may be documented through the record systems permitted by the statute.
Because a designee may participate in making the offer, a technician may also provide the pharmacist counseling if the patient later changes their mind.

questions.stem: A less expensive drug product is reasonably available and appears on the Massachusetts interchangeable-drug list, but the prescription contains a valid prescriber no-substitution direction. Which statements correctly describe the product-selection decision? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The valid no-substitution direction prevents the pharmacist from applying the usual required interchange on this prescription.
A lower price does not override a valid prescriber no-substitution direction.

Without a valid no-substitution direction, the Massachusetts interchange framework generally requires use of the reasonably available, less expensive interchangeable product when its conditions are met.
The patient may erase the prescriber's valid no-substitution direction and compel interchange without prescriber involvement.
Before interchanging, the pharmacist must still confirm that the alternative satisfies the Massachusetts interchangeable-product framework rather than relying on price alone.

questions.stem: A patient returns an unopened bottle that a Massachusetts pharmacy dispensed in error. The product appears intact. Which actions are required or permitted for the returned medication? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Accept the return because it was previously dispensed in error by the pharmacy.
Do not place the returned medication back into dispensing inventory merely because the container is unopened.
Segregate or quarantine the returned medication and handle its disposition under the pharmacy's required return/disposal process.
Keep the returned medication out of active dispensing inventory while it awaits proper disposition.
Dispense the returned bottle to another patient after a pharmacist visually inspects the seal.

content_boundary: Intentionally excludes keyed answers, explanations, rule/drug links, lifecycle fields, and all prior-review classifications so the auditor can solve independently first.
